newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Second Australia govt politician investigated.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Second Australia govt politician investigated.

text.p: A second Australian politician is being investigated by police over possible misuse of his parliamentary expense account, Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Sunday.
Howard said Michael Cobb, a parliamentarian in the town of Broken Hill, was being investigated over his expenses.
He said Cobb's electoral office had been raided last year by police and that the investigation was continuing.
Last week, Bob Woods, who held the junior position of parliamentary health secretary, resigned from politics amid charges that he fiddled his expenses.
Woods, who is also embroiled in a fight with his former lover who has taken out a restraining order on him, has denied any wrongdoing.
"I understand Michael Cobb's denied the allegations," Howard told the Channel Nine television's Sunday programme. "He, like Bob Woods, is entitled to a presumption of innocence."

Howard has been forced to defend himself and his year-old Liberal-National coalition government's code of conduct after he was accused last week, by the opposition Labor Party, of misleading the public over when he first heard about the police investigation into Woods.
Howard initially said he became aware of the investigation this month, but later told Parliament he had forgotten that he had been informed of the probe late last year.
The Woods expenses investigation has been clouded by media reports of his personal life. The private lives of politicians are usually not a political concern in Australian parliamentary debate.
On Sunday, Howard said he did not sit in moral judgement of his ministers.

"It's my view very strongly that (a minister's personal life) only becomes relevant where it directly interferes with the performance of their public duty or in some way it involves the taxpayer being done in the eye," Howard said.
"Then I think it is a perfectly understandable thing that it should come into the public domain," he said.

"I expect individuals in my government and in my ministry to behave correctly and behave properly, but I don't, like some kind of threatening father confessor, seek to sit in judgment on them, and I don't think the Australian public would want me to do that."
During last year's election campaign Howard vowed to lift parliamentary standards and developed a strict code of ministerial conduct once in office.

But his government came under attack early in its term after several ministers were questioned about their share portfolios and potential conflicts of interest in their business dealings, prompting the resignation of two junior government members.
